---
title: Estimating the ambulance pool
---

The model requires a single number representing how many ambulances exist in its resource pool. Because the model uses a fixed pool, this number remains constant at every simulated minute.

## Estimating the pool size from total weekly ambulance hours

The available data provide the total number of ambulance-hours per week. One ambulance staffed continuously for a full week provides:

$$
24 \times 7 = 168\text{ ambulance hours per week}
$$

Therefore, if the service provides 50,400 ambulance-hours per week:

$$
\frac{50,400\text{ ambulance hours per week}}{168\text{ hours per week}} = 300 \text{ ambulances}
$$

This doesn't mean there are 300 ambulances per day. Instead, it means that the **weekly staffing supplies capacity equivalent to 300 ambulances operating concurrently**.

## Multi-resource incidents

The model assigns one ambulance to each incident. However, in reality, many incidents will require multiple resources.

For example, for an incident requiring 3 resources, the model captures ambulance 1 but is omitting the workload of ambulances 2 and 3. This means it is underestimating resource utilisation and overestimating ambulance availability.

To compensate for this, the workload of second, third, and subsequent ambulances is converted into an **average concurrent ambulance equivalent** and subtracted from the fixed pool.

### Example calculation

For example, suppose there are ten Category 1 incidents on an average day, each incident uses two ambulances, and the mean ambulance job duration is 100 minutes.

The model already represents one ambulance per incident, so the omitted resources per incident are:

$$
2 - 1 = 1 \text{ additional ambulance}
$$

The total omitted workload is:

$$
10 \text{ incidents} \times 1 \text{ additional ambulance} \times 100 \text{ minutes} = 1000 \text{ additional ambulance minutes per day}
$$

One ambulance continuously occupied for a complete day accounts for:

$$
1 \times 24 \times 7 = 1440 \text{ minutes per day}
$$

Therefore, the omitted workload is equivalent to:

$$
\frac{1000 \text{ ambulance minutes per day}}{1440 \text{ minutes per day}} = 0.694 \text{ ambulances}
$$

So those extra Category 1 responses consume the same amount of capacity as 0.694 ambulances being continuously occupied throughout the day.
